name: Hanafuda (花札)
description: Hanafuda (花札, 'flower cards') are traditional Japanese playing cards comprising a 48-card deck divided into 12 suits, each representing a month and featuring a specific flower or plant. Hanafuda is not a single game but a family of games, most commonly fishing/capture games where players match cards from their hand with cards on the field. Popular games include Koi-Koi, Hachi-Hachi, and Hana-Awase. Cards are categorized as Brights, Animals, Ribbons, and Plains, with varying point values.

overview.description: Hanafuda (花札, 'flower cards') are traditional Japanese playing cards comprising a 48-card deck divided into 12 suits, each representing a month and featuring a specific flower or plant. Hanafuda is not a single game but a family of games, most commonly fishing/capture games where players match cards from their hand with cards on the field. Popular games include Koi-Koi, Hachi-Hachi, and Hana-Awase. Cards are categorized as Brights, Animals, Ribbons, and Plains, with varying point values.

history.origins: Hanafuda cards originated in 18th-century Japan, evolving from Portuguese playing cards. The Japanese government banned Western-style cards, leading to the development of Hanafuda as a workaround.
timeline: 16th Century: Portuguese traders introduce playing cards to Japan.
18th Century: Hanafuda cards developed to circumvent gambling bans.
19th Century: Hanafuda becomes widespread in Japan.
1889: Nintendo founded as a Hanafuda card manufacturer.
Present: Hanafuda remains popular in Japan, Korea (Hwatu), and Hawaii.
history.cultural: Hanafuda is deeply embedded in Japanese culture, associated with traditional festivals and family gatherings. Nintendo, now a video game giant, started as a Hanafuda card company.
history.evolution: Hanafuda evolved from Portuguese cards, with Japanese artisans replacing Western suits with seasonal flowers and plants. The 12-suit structure represents the 12 months of the year.

setup.players: 2 to 6 players depending on the specific Hanafuda game (e.g. Koi-Koi typically 2).
setup.deck:
48 cards divided into 12 suits (months):
- January (Pine), February (Plum), March (Cherry), April (Wisteria), May (Iris), June (Peony), July (Bush Clover), August (Pampas Grass), September (Chrysanthemum), October (Maple), November (Willow), December (Paulownia).

Each suit has 4 cards, categorized as:
- **Brights** (20 points): Special high-value cards.
- **Animals** (10 points): Cards featuring animals.
- **Ribbons** (5 points): Cards with ribbons or poetry.
- **Plains/Chaff** (1 point): Simple flower cards.
setup.dealing: Varies by game; typically dealer distributes cards to hands and table.

rules.objective: Varies by game; in fishing games capture matching cards; in Koi-Koi form yaku and decide to continue or stop for points.
rules.gameplay: Varies by game. In fishing games players match hand cards with table cards to capture. In Koi-Koi players form point combinations (yaku) and choose to continue or stop.
keyRules: Hanafuda is a family of games; each variant has its own rules.
48 cards in 12 suits (months), 4 cards per suit.
Card types: Brights, Animals, Ribbons, Plains.

strategy.basic: Focus on capturing high-value cards (Brights, Animals, Ribbons). Learn the basic yaku for your chosen game.
strategy.intermediate: Track which cards have been played to anticipate remaining cards. Decide when to stop (in Koi-Koi) vs. continue for more yaku.
strategy.advanced: Memorize all yaku and their values. Calculate exact point differentials. Bluff opponents by capturing cards that suggest you're building a specific yaku.
